content: The primary function of poison centers is clinical in nature, focusing on providing advice and, in some cases, treatment for poisoning incidents. Poison centers vary in structure and function globally, but at a minimum, they serve as information services. Some poison centers also include clinical treatment units and/or laboratories capable of performing toxicological analyses. The data collected by poison centers during their operations can be utilized for public health purposes and to support the sound management of chemicals through toxicovigilance. Additional roles of poison centers may include organizing antidote supplies, participating in research, education, and training, and advising on environmental exposure to chemical substances. Community engagement is often an important activity to raise awareness about poison centers. In some countries, poison centers address toxicological issues affecting both humans and animals. Poisoning in animals can have significant economic consequences, leading to the establishment of veterinary poison information centers in countries such as Australia, France, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Different terms are used worldwide to describe services that provide information and advice on poisoning management, treatment, and laboratory services. These include poisons information center, poisons information service, poison control center, poisons information and support center, antipoison center, poison center, toxicology information service, and toxicology center. In this guidance, the term poisons information center refers to establishments providing only information and advice, while poison center refers to those that also include clinical treatment units and/or toxicological laboratories. The term poison center is also used generically when the discussion applies to both types of establishments. Specialist staff working in poison centers include specialists in poisons information, who are health service professionals trained to provide information and advice on the diagnosis and management of poisoning, and medical toxicologists, who are medical doctors with specialized training in clinical toxicology. After World War II, the rapid development of new chemical products, including pharmaceuticals and pesticides, led to a significant increase in poisoning cases. This highlighted the need for specialist toxicology advice, prompting the establishment of poison centers. The first clinical toxicology treatment units preceded the creation of poisons information centers. One of the earliest treatment centers was established in 1949 at Bispebjerg Hospital in Denmark, primarily treating patients with psychotropic drug overdoses. Centralizing poisoning treatment and focusing on clinical monitoring were credited with reducing mortality rates from poisoning. In the United States, the evolution of poisons information centers was driven by the high rate of fatal poisonings among young children, as revealed by an epidemiological study conducted in 1949–1950. The first poisons information center in the world was established in Chicago in 1953, providing professional telephone advice and using a standardized data collection form. The first European poisons information center was founded in the Netherlands in 1960. Subsequently, more centers were established, particularly in Asia, Australasia, Europe, and North America. Early poisons information centers drew expertise from various medical specialties, including pediatrics, intensive care, forensic medicine, occupational health, analytical toxicology, pharmacy, and pharmacology. While the original character of many centers has been maintained, there is considerable heterogeneity in their structure and organization. Historically, poison centers provided advice in response to telephone inquiries, but more recently, internet-based databases have become prominent in some countries. Poisons information centers collect data on referred cases to characterize the frequency and patterns of poisoning in the population and for medico-legal purposes. Advances in information technology have enabled the establishment of poison center surveillance systems for aggregating, analyzing, and interpreting national data on poisoning. These datasets can inform public health initiatives and regulatory measures for poisoning prevention and harm reduction. The establishment of poison centers has been recognized as a priority in international health and environmental forums. For example, Agenda 21, adopted at the 1992 United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, emphasized the importance of poison centers. The Intergovernmental Forum on Chemical Safety, established in 1994, reiterated this priority in its action plans. The International Health Regulations (IHR) require countries to have the capacity to detect, alert, and respond to public health events caused by chemicals, including access to poisons information centers and toxicology laboratory services. Poisons information centers are specialized units that respond to inquiries, often via telephone, about exposure to chemical agents, including pharmaceuticals, substances of abuse, natural toxins, pesticides, and industrial chemicals. They assess whether an exposure is hazardous and provide tailored advice on treatment, ensuring it is evidence-based and discouraging ineffective or unnecessary interventions. In complex or severe cases, specialists in poisons information can refer callers to medical toxicologists for detailed clinical advice. Poison centers may also advise on the necessity of laboratory analyses and the availability of antidotes. As centers of toxicology expertise, poisons information centers assist in diagnosing patients with acute symptoms of unknown origin. In some countries, such as New Zealand, South Africa, and the United Kingdom, poison centers have developed internet-based clinical toxicology databases for health professionals managing straightforward poisoning cases. A limited number of online resources are also available for public use. For example, in the United States, an online and smartphone application provides basic first aid and advice on poisons, serving as a triage mechanism to reduce unnecessary medical referrals and ensure urgent care when needed. Poisons information centers have pioneered teleconsultation and are increasingly using telemedicine techniques, such as audio-visual consultations with patients. These methods are particularly useful in locations without a medical toxicologist or when consultation with a specialist adviser, such as a snakebite expert, is required. Telemedicine consultations can prevent unnecessary patient transport to distant hospitals, expedite diagnosis and treatment, and reduce healthcare costs. In areas with poor telecommunications infrastructure, poison centers may conduct direct consultations with individuals who visit in person, although this is uncommon. They may also provide written materials, such as treatment algorithms in poster form, and use other communication channels, such as emails, letters, and social media, for non-urgent inquiries. In addition to providing information, poisons information centers collect data on poisoning cases, including circumstances and severity. This data collection and analysis are part of toxicovigilance activities, helping to identify unanticipated hazards of chemicals and products and the emergence of new toxicological risks. These data can also enhance knowledge about the toxicity of various agents, identify failures in risk management, and inform prevention efforts. Poisons information centers collaborate with other organizations to detect, prepare for, and respond to chemical incidents. They may also provide information on toxic chemicals, including environmental risks and safe levels in food and environmental media, to a wide range of users, including medical professionals, government authorities, the media, and the public. Severely poisoned patients may require rapid transportation to an appropriate hospital or the presence of a specially trained doctor if immediate movement is not possible. Poison centers may need to be aware of the availability of paramedics and transport options. Formal communication arrangements between poison centers and ambulance services can assist with triaging patients during large-scale poisoning incidents. Ideally, poisons information services should be available 24/7 throughout the year to address poisoning incidents promptly.
